tagline.text: Ten steps from the beach, a sea where millions of sardines dance

children.text: A diving village on Cebu's southwest coast, where swimming just a few dozen meters out from Panagsama Beach brings you face to face with millions of sardines and sea turtles. You can also pair it with diving at Pescador Island and canyoneering at Kawasan Falls, making it one of Cebu's most rewarding coastal destinations.
Moalboal is a coastal town about
90km

southwest of Cebu City, facing Negros Island across the Tañon Strait. Travelers gather at Panagsama Beach, a short distance west of the town center, where dive shops, guesthouses, and restaurants line the shore. Known among divers since the 1970s and 80s, it's also one of the Philippines' oldest diving villages.

What made Moalboal world-famous is the sardine swarm known as the "Sardine Run." An estimated several million sardines form a huge school along the coral wall (drop-off) right off Panagsama Beach, and unlike other regions where the fish migrate seasonally, they stay in this spot nearly all year round. Just walk into the water from the beach with snorkel gear and swim out
to witness the spectacle of a silver wall of fish shifting direction like a whirlwind right in front of you.

Sea turtles are another Moalboal specialty. Green sea turtles often appear in the seagrass beds off Panagsama and around nearby White Beach (Basdaku), so even just snorkeling lets you watch turtles surface for air up close. Pescador Island, about
3km
off the coast, is a marine sanctuary with coral walls, caves, and a variety of tropical fish, making it a must-visit spot for divers.
Divers will love it, of course, but even snorkelers without a diving certification will be plenty impressed. Kawasan Falls canyoneering is about
30 minutes

away by car, and it can also be combined with the Oslob whale sharks in a single-day itinerary, making it a good base for a southern Cebu trip. In the evening, the atmosphere of watching the sunset at a beach bar and mingling with backpackers from around the world is also part of the appeal.
Moalboal is a municipality of 15 barangays with 37,993 residents as of the
census (area about 125 km²), and Panagsama lies in its Basdiot barangay. In
December 2021
, Typhoon Odette (Rai) heavily damaged the shallow coral at depths of about
or less, which is still recovering, but the sardine run and the deep coral wall were unaffected and can still be seen as before. The epicenter of the
September 30, 2025
Cebu earthquake was in Bogo in the north, and the Department of Tourism said Cebu's tourist sites remain open; during Typhoon Kalmaegi (Tino) in
November 2025
, diving in Moalboal was also briefly suspended. Check the latest conditions before you set out.

Rent gear at Panagsama Beach and enter the water right from the beach steps or in front of a resort. Swim out to where the coral cliff begins, and you'll find the sardines massed close to the surface, a giant silver cloud passing beneath your feet.
Early morning gives you the best chance of encountering turtles in the seagrass beds off Panagsama or White Beach. Keep a distance of at least several meters and observe quietly.

blocks.title: Hopping and diving at Pescador Island

children.text: Take a bangka to the Pescador Island marine sanctuary and snorkel or dive along its coral walls. An underwater cave near the island called the "Cathedral" is famous among divers.
Panagsama has dozens of dive shops, some with Korean instructors. Diving right inside the sardine run is an experience unique to Moalboal.
Panagsama has almost no sandy beach, so swimming is done at White Beach in Basdaku to the north. It's about
15 minutes
away by tricycle, with fine sand and a shallow sea.
A canyoneering tour that picks you up from your Moalboal accommodation, jumping and swimming down the canyon all the way to Kawasan Falls. Most Moalboal travelers spend a full day on this.

blocks.title: Sunset and beach bars at Panagsama

children.text: Moalboal's coast faces west, so at dusk the sun sets over Negros Island. Finish the day at a beach bar with a bottle of San Miguel.
At the Panagsama house reef, you walk in from in front of a dive shop for a shore dive that brings you to the sardines and turtles, and night dives are possible too. Pescador Island is about
15–20 minutes

away by boat, with a wall that drops past the shallow coral at 3–10m to depths of more than 55m, plus the "Cathedral" cave. Wall dives at Tongo Point, Tuble, and in front of White Beach take 10–20 minutes by boat, and Sunken Island, with its strong currents, is for experienced divers. Boat dives cost about
each, and many operators charge a marine park fee of
separately.

On days when the southwest monsoon is strong, the Coast Guard stops bangkas from leaving, and after heavy rain Kawasan canyoneering may also be suspended. Leave one day of your itinerary free for tours, and check with your accommodation or dive shop the previous evening whether boats are running.
The nearest airport is Mactan-Cebu International Airport (CEB), with direct flights from Incheon and Busan, and many domestic flights from Manila (about
1 hour 20 minutes
). From the airport to Moalboal takes about
3–4 hours
by car; booking a private vehicle or van costs about
. You can also call a Grab all the way to Moalboal, but the fare is expensive and it's hard to get a car assigned.

At the South Bus Terminal on N. Bacalso Avenue in Cebu City, board a Ceres bus on the "Bato via Barili" route and get off at Moalboal. The "Bato via Oslob" bus, which runs along the opposite east coast, goes in a different direction and takes a long detour, so be sure to check the destination sign. Sources differ on the first bus (3–5 AM) and the last (about 6–9 PM), with departures roughly every
30 minutes
in between. The trip takes about
3–4 hours
depending on traffic, and fares are about
for an air-conditioned bus and about
for an ordinary bus. Vans (V-Hire) from the same terminal leave when full, costing about
and taking
2 hours 30 minutes–3 hours 30 minutes

, but the seats are cramped. In Moalboal, get off in front of the Jollibee across from the municipal hall in the town center; on the way back to Cebu, flag down the bus in front of it. From the airport to the bus terminal is about
40 minutes–1 hour
by taxi or Grab.
The Cebu BRT, in partial service since
March 2026

, stops at the South Bus Terminal, so if you're staying around IT Park, Ayala, the Capitol, or Fuente Osmeña, you can also take the BRT to the terminal. For the first bus at dawn, a taxi or Grab is the safer choice; check the latest announcements for BRT operating hours and fares.
From Cebu City, take the south coastal road to Carcar, then head west past Barili through Dumanjug, Ronda, and Alcantara to reach Moalboal. The distance is about
and it normally takes about
2 hours 30 minutes–3 hours
, with
30 minutes–1 hour
more on weekends and holidays. Leaving before 7 AM helps you avoid the traffic. A private van booked in Cebu City costs about
From Tagbilaran in Bohol, a fast ferry such as OceanJet takes about
2 hours
to the Cebu City port, with fares of about

depending on seat class. From the port you need to take a taxi or Grab to the South Bus Terminal and change to a bus, so you'll need an early boat to reach Moalboal the same day. Check the latest announcements for ferry schedules and fares.
Coming from Dumaguete, the Bato (Samboan)–Tampi route is the closest to Moalboal. Maayo Shipping ferries run seven trips a day (first boat
, last boat
) and take about
30 minutes
. The fare is about
, though sources differ and a fuel surcharge may apply, so confirm at the ticket window at the pier. Tampi is about
30 minutes
north of Dumaguete, and from Bato a Ceres bus takes about
1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes
to Moalboal. There's also a route from Sibulan port next to Dumaguete to Liloan (Santander) (nine trips a day), but for Moalboal the Bato–Tampi route is closer.
From the Moalboal bus stop (town center) to Panagsama is about
10 minutes
by tricycle, costing around
. It's easy to get around the beach on foot, and for nearby trips to White Beach or Kawasan, charter a tricycle or habal-habal. Scooter rental is also available for about
a day. To cross to Negros, take a ferry from Bato port to the south, crossing to Tampi near Dumaguete.
The sardine run can be seen almost year-round, but the dry season,
December–May
, with calm seas and good visibility, is best. In
March–May
, water temperatures rise to 29–30°C, so you won't feel cold even after long periods in the water. In
December–February
, temperatures drop slightly to 26–27°C, so a 3mm wetsuit or rash guard is handy.
June–November
is the rainy season with frequent afternoon showers, and when the southwest monsoon blows, waves rise along west-facing Panagsama, which can cloud visibility. During typhoon season (mainly
August–November
), bangka tours and canyoneering can be suspended. Still, walk-in snorkeling from the shore is possible year-round as long as sea conditions are fine.
Visibility is about
in the dry season, sometimes exceeding
in March–May, and drops to about
in the rainy season. In the
December–February
peak season, it's best to book accommodation and dive shops
2–3 months
ahead, and it is also crowded during Holy Week and the Christmas and New Year holidays. Around
May 16
, the coral-themed Moalboal Kagasangan Festival is held.

Accommodation around Panagsama Beach is the most convenient. The sardine run spot is a few minutes' walk away, and dive shops, restaurants, and bars are all clustered together. Dorms run about
a night, private-room guesthouses about
, and dive resorts with pools about
. If you want a quiet beach retreat, choosing a resort on the White Beach side is also a good option.

The Panagsama restaurant row has a surprisingly wide range of options for such a small town — Filipino home cooking, seafood barbecue, European brunch, pizza, and even Thai and Mexican food, with vegetarian options common too. Near the public market in Moalboal town, you can find cheap lechon and local dishes. Southern Cebu specialties like mangoes and banana snacks are also easy to find on the street.

Panagsama has dozens of dive shops, so compare each shop's PADI rating, boat size, and group size when choosing. Savedra Dive Center and Cebu Fun Divers are known as PADI 5-Star operators, and Quo Vadis Dive Resort runs both accommodation and diving. After dark, many travelers spend the evening at beach bars such as Chili Bar, which has a pool table. On the White Beach side, private rooms start at around
, so budget travelers have options too. Business conditions can change, so confirm before booking.
The sardine run tends to gather closer to the surface in the early morning and late afternoon, and there are fewer people around, making it a good time for photos.
The beach entry points are a slippery mix of rock and coral. Wear aqua shoes or fins when going in.
A waterproof camera or action cam makes footage of the sardine run the best souvenir. Action cam rental is also available locally.
There's an ATM in Panagsama too, but it's often out of order or out of cash. Withdraw plenty in Moalboal town or Cebu beforehand.
Air-conditioned buses are more comfortable, but the AC can be strong, so bring a light jacket.
Booking canyoneering the day before through your accommodation or a dive shop is convenient, since pickup is included.
If you want to see the Oslob whale sharks too, a private vehicle tour departing Moalboal at dawn lets you do it all in a day.

Register for the environmental user fee at the kiosk at the entrance to Panagsama beach or at the tourist information office, and keep the receipt. Residents, seniors, people with disabilities, and children aged 10 and under are exempt, and those who have booked diving or hopping must still get a pass.
Most businesses in Panagsama accept cash only. The town has Landbank, BDO, BPI, and PNB branches, so withdraw during banking hours.
Wi-Fi on the beach is slow and often drops, so prepare Smart or Globe SIM or eSIM data.
The depth suddenly increases in front of the coral wall where the sardine run is. Wear a life vest if you're not a confident swimmer.
The area off the beach is also a bangka route, so wear a surface marker buoy or bright-colored clothing while snorkeling and watch out for boats.
Touching or chasing sea turtles is prohibited and can result in a fine.
Instead of chemical sunscreen that harms coral, use a rash guard and reef-safe products.
There are seasons when jellyfish appear, so a long-sleeve rash guard is recommended.
Touching marine life or coral, fishing, cutting buoys, or dumping trash can result in a fine of about
per offense under local ordinance, and marine wardens enforce this.
Marine sanctuary entrance fees and rules change from time to time. Check the latest fees before hopping or diving.
